facts.claim: "HOPE" was released on February 16, 2023, as the lead single from NF's fifth studio album, also called HOPE.
Nate Feuerstein (NF) wrote the song with Tommee Profitt. The two produced it with Jeff Sojka.
Songfacts credits Patrick Tohill as a co-producer as well. Tohill is better known as a director and is NF's regular visual collaborator.
On the album, Tommee Profitt handled mixing and programming for the title track.
The song opens with plucky piano chords. It moves into staccato strings and a pulsing echo of background voices.
The music video came out the same day as the song. NF and Patrick Tohill directed it.
In the video, competing voices (NF's old self and new self) fight over whose album it will be. The new self wins and names the album "HOPE".

The single is NF's first release of 2023. Universal Music Canada's press release says it finds him assessing his musical journey so far and looking ahead. It is the lead single from his first album since 2019's The Search and his first longer project since the 2021 mixtape CLOUDS (THE MIXTAPE).
NME reported that the song reached 32 million global streams in its first week.
In an NME interview, NF described writing and recording as "therapy" and "an outlet" for him.

research.lineage: The song sits in NF's confessional, mental-health-focused Christian-rooted hip-hop, which press often compares to Eminem-style rap, and it marks a turn toward optimism and new beginnings.

draft:
Partway through **HOPE**, NF fires himself. "Nate, you've had a great run," he says, with the cool courtesy of a manager clearing out a desk, and then a new voice steps up to introduce the album. It plays as a bit, but it isn't a joke. The self being let go spent thirty years dragging his feet and blaming everyone else, and the self doing the firing still sounds like he's apologizing: "I don't want you to feel like a failure / I know this hurts." Pride and tenderness share the same breath. He's cutting loose a version of himself he still feels sorry for.

The music stays out of the way so that argument can land. Plucky piano chords open it, a simple, melancholy figure that keeps circling while a synth bass holds long notes underneath and a pad fills the air. Kick and snare come in plain and unfussy. The mix is clean and dry, the vocal right up front with no harmonies to soften it, and the track builds by stacking layers rather than by any big swing. Staccato strings and a pulsing echo of background voices arrive as it goes. NF wrote the song with Tommee Profitt, who also handled mixing and programming, and the two produced it with Jeff Sojka. Patrick Tohill, NF's regular director, gets a co-production credit as well.

The verses start as a pep talk, a definition of success built from grinding and dreaming big, and then they get heavier. NF calls a mental breakdown the push that got him into help. He picks up his son every morning and promises the boy will never be the kid at the window wondering whether dad is coming. Then he catches himself, says that wasn't a shot, and adds, "Mama, I forgive you." Forgiveness and the old injury sit in the same bar. He can't say one without the other showing.

Then comes the pileup: thirty years of shame, of anger, of fake, of chains, ending on thirty years of pushing everyone away. After that, the doubting voice speaks in parentheses and NF answers it line for line until it cuts him off mid-sentence. He finishes anyway, with one word: reins. The video, which NF co-directed with Tohill, stages the same fight between his old self and new self over whose album this will be.

It's the confessional, Christian-rooted rap NF has built his name on, the kind press often holds up against Eminem. He keeps the device of arguing with yourself on record and bends it toward optimism. He has called writing "therapy," and this song sounds like a session that ends on a breakthrough.

What sticks is hearing someone forgive the people who hurt him, himself included, then grab the last word before the old voice can finish, so you feel hope arrive as an argument he wins.
